questions.question: What is the difference between `@Component` and `@ComponentScan`?
options: `@Component` creates the container, while `@ComponentScan` creates the beans
They are interchangeable; either one alone makes a class a bean
`@Component` marks a class as eligible to become a bean; `@ComponentScan` tells Spring which packages to search for such classes
`@ComponentScan` goes on each bean class, while `@Component` goes on the configuration class
questions.explanation: `@Component` is a class-level marker saying "this class may be a Spring bean"; `@ComponentScan` (typically on the `@Configuration` class) tells Spring where to look - the given package and its sub-packages. Writing `@Component` alone is not enough if no scan covers that package.

questions.question: Why does `ApplicationContext context = new ApplicationContext();` fail to compile, and what does the lecture use instead?
options: `ApplicationContext` is an interface, so you instantiate an implementation such as `new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class)`
Its constructor is private; you must call `ApplicationContext.getInstance()`
It needs the `spring-boot` dependency; plain Spring has no container
It is an abstract annotation; you must annotate `Main` with `@ApplicationContext`
questions.explanation: `ApplicationContext` is an interface representing the IoC container, and interfaces cannot be instantiated. For annotation-based configuration the lecture uses its implementation `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext`, passing the configuration class. `spring-context` alone is enough - no Spring Boot needed.

questions.question: You want Spring to manage an `EmailClient` object from a third-party JAR. You cannot edit that class, and its constructor needs an API key string. How do you register it?
options: Add `@Component` to `EmailClient` in your copy of the JAR
Add the library's package to `@ComponentScan`; Spring will guess the API key
Call `new EmailClient(key)` in `main()`; Spring registers every created object automatically
Write a `@Bean` method in your `@Configuration` class that returns `new EmailClient(key)`
questions.explanation: `@Bean` is for exactly this case: classes you cannot annotate (external libraries) or whose creation needs custom values. Spring calls the method and registers the returned object as a bean. Scanning cannot help because the class has no `@Component` and Spring would not know what string to pass; objects created with `new` are not beans.

questions.question: This is the lecture's configuration (`CardPayment` is also annotated with `@Component` and lies inside `in.coderarmy`). What does `Main` print?
options:
Order placed
Paying via card

Paying via card
Order placed

Paying by UPI
Order placed
Startup fails: three `PaymentService` beans make the injection ambiguous
questions.explanation: There are three `PaymentService` beans (scanned `cardPayment`, `createCardPayment`, `createUpiPayment`), but `@Qualifier("cp")` narrows the candidates to the one bean carrying that qualifier, `createCardPayment`, so there is no ambiguity. `placeOrder()` calls `pay()` before printing, giving "Paying via card" then "Order placed".

questions.question: Given this configuration, which lookup returns the `User` bean?
options: `context.getBean("user")`
`context.getBean("createUser")`
`context.getBean("userBean")`
`context.getBean("appConfig.createUser")`
questions.explanation: For `@Bean` methods the default bean name is the method name, so the bean is called `createUser`. The class-name-based name `user` is what you would get from `@Component` on `User`, which is not used here. A custom name would need `@Bean("user")`; `getBean(User.class)` would also work by type.

questions.question: `AppConfig` has `@ComponentScan("in.coderarmy")`. A teammate adds `@Component public class UpiPayment implements PaymentService` in package `com.thirdparty.pay`, and `OrderService` (a `@Component` in `in.coderarmy`) needs a `PaymentService`. Startup fails with "No qualifying bean of type 'PaymentService' available". What is the cause?
options: `com.thirdparty.pay` is outside the scanned package, so `UpiPayment` was never registered as a bean
`@Component` cannot be used on classes that implement an interface
`OrderService` must use field injection to find beans in other packages
Interfaces need their own `@Component`, so `PaymentService` must be annotated too
questions.explanation: Component scanning covers only the given package and its sub-packages; `com.thirdparty.pay` is not under `in.coderarmy`, so the class is never found and no `PaymentService` bean exists. Fix it by adding that package to `@ComponentScan` or registering the object with a `@Bean` method. The injection style does not change which beans exist.

questions.question: Why does the lecture discourage `@Autowired private PaymentService paymentService;` (field injection) for required dependencies?
options: Because field injection only works for `public` fields
Because Spring cannot use reflection to set private fields
Because field injection creates a new `PaymentService` for every method call
Because the dependency is hidden, the field cannot be `final`, and the class is hard to create in a plain unit test without Spring
questions.explanation: Field injection works - Spring sets even private fields via reflection - but the dependency is invisible from the constructor, the field cannot be `final`, the object can exist half-initialized, and tests need Spring (or reflection) to fill it. Constructor injection avoids all of that, which is why it is preferred for mandatory dependencies.

questions.question: Both payment classes are in a scanned package. What is printed when `orderService.placeOrder()` is called?
options:
UPI payment done
Order placed
Nothing - startup fails because `@Primary` and `@Qualifier` conflict

Card payment done
Order placed
Nothing - startup fails because no bean is named `cardPaymentService`
questions.explanation: `CardPaymentService` gets the default bean name `cardPaymentService`, so the qualifier matches it. `@Primary` is only a default choice; `@Qualifier` is a specific choice and wins, so the card implementation is injected. Using both is legal and does not cause a startup failure.

questions.question: `CardPayment` is annotated with `@Component` and is in the scanned package. A teammate also adds `@Bean public PaymentService createCardPayment() { return new CardPayment(); }` to `AppConfig` (no qualifiers anywhere). `OrderService` is a `@Component` with constructor `OrderService(PaymentService paymentService)`. What happens at startup?
options: Spring notices both describe `CardPayment` and silently keeps only one bean
The `@Bean` method is ignored because component scanning always takes priority
`OrderService` receives a new `CardPayment` created by calling the constructor directly
Two `PaymentService` beans exist (`cardPayment` and `createCardPayment`), so injecting by type is ambiguous and startup fails
questions.explanation: Registering the same class via `@Component` and via a `@Bean` method with a different name produces two separate beans. With two candidates and no `@Primary`/`@Qualifier` (and no bean named `paymentService`), Spring cannot choose and fails with a no-unique-bean error. The clean rule from the notes: register a bean with either `@Component` or `@Bean`, not both.

questions.question: During startup, Spring builds `BeanDefinition`s before creating any bean objects. What is a `BeanDefinition`, and why does Spring do this first?
options: It is the first instance of each bean, kept as a template to clone other instances from
It is the compiled `.class` file of the bean, loaded early so the JVM can verify it
It is metadata (class, name, scope, dependencies, creation strategy) that lets Spring know every bean and its needs before resolving dependencies and creating objects
It is a log entry recording that a bean was created, used later for debugging
questions.explanation: A `BeanDefinition` is not the object but information about how to create and manage it. Because Spring manages a whole application, it first collects which beans exist, their classes, scopes and dependencies, and only then creates objects in a workable order and injects dependencies. It is not an instance or a template copy.
